transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-10-30
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Hannah Park (Redwood AE), Diego Martinez (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood), Maya Ramesh (Ember CTO), Raj Patel (Ember ML Eng), Sofia Gomez (Ember Platform), Tom Wu (Ember Security)

Summary (auto): quick walkthrough of Redwood API, Console, and Optimize; parity mapping approach from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together models; security checklist and POC next steps.
Topics: API parity, model mapping, streaming & function-calling differences, cost/latency tradeoffs, private deployment constraints, Optimize recommendations for batching/quantization.

[00:00] Hannah (Redwood AE): Okay hi everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intros, real quick. I'm Hannah, AE on the Redwood side.
[00:08] Maya (Ember): Hey yeah Maya here. We're trying to move a bunch of inference from OpenAI and Anthropic into a single endpoint if poss— trying to avoid vendor lock and reduce cost.
[00:17] Raj (Ember): Hi, Raj; I'll be doing the integration work. We also have some function-calling heavy flows and streaming chat.
[00:24] Diego (Redwood SE): Great. Today we'll run through the API parity mapping, show the Console and Optimize hints, and then demo a short migration path. There will be some dev/deep-dive time at the end.
[00:33] Hannah: Quick ask — what are the must-haves? Latency? Preservation of outputs? Cost target?
[00:37] Sofia (Ember): Latency under 350ms p50 for short queries, p95 < 700ms ideally. And output must be semantically identical for our assistant flows — we have strict QA.
[00:47] Tom (Ember Security): SOC2 and audit logs are table stakes. If you have a private VPC option that helps. KMS integration is required.
[00:56] Diego: Noted. Redwood Dedicated / Private supports KMS/HSM and per-tenant audit logs. I'll show the security doc link after.

--- Transcript body (mist-transcribed bits and natural speech) ---
[01:15] Diego: So first, parity mapping. At the high level, we map model families. For example, your previous OpenAI usage of gpt-4o-ish or gpt-4-turbo you can map to our redwood-4o or to curated open models. Same with Anthropic claude-ish you can map to a high-safety variant. One thing to watch is sampling parameters — temperature, top_p, repetition penalty are the knobs.
[01:35] Maya: We use both deterministic (temp 0) and creative modes. Also function-calling semantics — we use structured tool calls, nested args sometimes.
[01:46] Diego: Yep. Redwood supports function calling and structured output; note that the JSON parsing heuristics are slightly different, so we recommend a small prompt shim and a deterministic test harness.
[01:58] Raj: How about streaming? We rely on server-sent events from OpenAI.
[02:03] Liam (Redwood): Our streaming is chunked over HTTP/2 with SSE-esque framing for SDKs; there are subtle differences in delta composition — you may see tokens split in different boundaries. Usually not an issue but unit tests catch those.
[02:17] Maya: Cool. Any gotchas with our existing role-based prompts?
[02:21] Diego: We saw customers swap role tokens for system messages; we have a compatibility layer that maps role arrays to our chat API.

[03:00] (Auto-generated: Topics — mapping table, console demo, Optimize suggestions, security stack)

[04:12] Diego: I'm going to share my screen and open the Console. Quick note: Console routes, model pinning, and rollout policies let you do canary traffic for a single route — that's handy for your progressive rollout.
[04:26] Diego: Here is the parity mapping spreadsheet skeleton — columns: source_provider, source_model, redwood_model_recommendation, prompt_shim, expected_delta_notes.
[04:38] Maya: Can you give a concrete example from our logs? We sent a sample trace earlier — a 3s multi-turn chat that calls two functions.
[04:46] Diego: Right, for that trace we recommend mapping OpenAI gpt-4o-mini to redwood-4o-mini-q8 with a shim to reduce repetition penalty and to shorten the user prefix. Quantization reduces cost but we keep a higher precision path for the last turn if you need exact deterministic outputs.
[05:04] Raj: Question — does quantization affect JSON output reliability?
[05:08] Diego: Slightly. In our experience q8 sometimes causes tokenization changes that can shift punctuation; for strict JSON we usually recommend q8_0 for earlier tokens but run final-turn decode on a higher-precision replica or fallback. Optimize can auto-suggest that.

[06:00] Hannah: On the cost side, can you ballpark our per-1M tokens after conversion?
[06:04] Diego: We did a rough estimate with your sample: hosted mode with redwood-4o-mini-q8 would be roughly ~65% of current OpenAI spend, depending on cache hit rate and batching. Dedicated pricing differs — you commit and get a predictable unit cost.
[06:21] Maya: What about throughput? Our peak is around 100 concurrent short chat requests.
[06:27] Diego: Dedicated pools support scaling to that easily; autoscaling and burst capacity are configurable. For hosted, we route to different capacity tiers to meet SLA.

[07:10] Tom (Security): Where do logs live? We need immutable audit log for requests and response hashes.
[07:16] Liam: We can push logs to your SIEM (Splunk/Datadog) and store audit trails in your VPC. We also support response-hash-only logging to avoid PII storage. KMS integration available for envelope encryption.

[08:30] Raj: Integration detail: we call OpenAI with function_call: "auto" and the model returns a function payload. What will change?
[08:40] Diego: The behavior is similar; we support function_name in the response. One caveat — our function schema validation is strict and we encourage you to include JSON schema in the tool def to reduce parse ambiguity. You'll need to add a small shim to existing code (two lines) that checks for the response.

[09:55] Maya: Can we run side-by-side A/B for a week?
[09:59] Hannah: Yes, you can route a portion of traffic to Redwood and compare results. Console has per-route traffic split and trace comparison.

[11:10] Diego: Now quick demo of Optimize — this is where we ingest your trace and suggest batching, cache windows, and quantization profiles. For your high-frequency short queries, Optimize suggests: prefix caching for the top 20 intents, max_batch_size 32, and a q8 middle path.
[11:32] Raj: Explain prefix caching — is it safe for personalized prompts?
[11:36] Diego: Prefix caching caches the model KV state for common system+user prefix up to the personalization token. For personalization we recommend cache keys that include user-id hash to avoid leakage. Optimize auto-recommends TTLs based on per-intent variance.

[13:00] Sofia: What about rollout testing? Can we diff responses automatically?
[13:06] Liam: Yes, Console can run automatic regression detection over a sample eval set and raise alerts for semantic drift or token-level changes. We also have a ways to store golden outputs for exact-match checks.

[15:20] (Some cross talk)
[15:33] Raj: We have a lot of prompt engineering — do you support prompt templating in the Console?
[15:38] Diego: Yes, prompt sets and secret-managed templates are available. You can bind them to routes so code calls an endpoint name instead of raw prompt text.

[18:10] Maya: Anything special for Anthropic -> Redwood? We saw safety layers in Claude we rely on.
[18:18] Diego: For Anthropic-type safety behavior we map to a safety curated model and add a system-level instruction shim. Also Redwood has safety filters you can opt into; we capture false-positive/negative feedback for tuning.

[20:00] Hannah: Quick product question — how do you handle usage spikes?
[20:03] Diego: Autoscaling, warm pools for Dedicated, on-hosted we have soft-fallbacks to cheaper models or other regions according to your policy. Fallbacks preserve basic semantics but could be slightly different; we recommend canary + alerting for that.

[22:15] Maya: About latency — you said p50 350ms target — what steps to verify?
[22:20] Diego: We can run benchmark harness in your VPC or ours. Typical short-turns with 512 token windows hit the cited p50 on our recommended instance types; we'll share the benchmark spreadsheet and raw traces.

[25:00] (Diego shares a quick CLI example)
[25:12] Diego: Example curl to the Redwood API: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <key>" -d '{"model":"redwood-4o-mini-q8","messages":[{"role":"system","content":"..."},{"role":"user","content":"..."}]}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat/completions
[25:36] Raj: Will the SDK handle token accounting like OpenAI?
[25:40] Diego: Yes, SDK and Console show per-request token breakdown and cost. We also provide token-level latency breakdown in the Console traces.

[28:00] Maya: Any pitfalls with embeddings differences? We use OpenAI-embedding-text-2 for semantic search.
[28:07] Diego: We have a recommended embeddings family; similarity distance can shift slightly. We advise re-indexing and running a small eval to pick a threshold. Optimize can run the embedding reharmonization test for you.

[30:40] Sofia: Security again — what about VPC egress rules and private control plane?
[30:45] Liam: Private deployment gives you a customer-managed control plane; egress is over your egress IPs and we can support air-gapped options for on-prem installs.

[33:00] (Transcript shows a small misrecognized phrase)
[33:05] Tom (Security): Could you send the SOC2 attestation?
[33:08] Hannah: Yes I will share the security pack after, plus a short checklist for your compliance team.

[36:12] Diego: Re: regression testing — here's our suggested POC plan: 1) ingest top 500 prompt examples, 2) run side-by-side parity evals for N metrics (semantic similarity, exact-match for functions, latency), 3) iterate prompt shims for top 10 failing cases, 4) gradually increase traffic with canary.
[36:35] Raj: That sounds good. How long to set up the POC?
[36:38] Hannah: We aim for 1-2 weeks to get a staging key + ingestion + first eval depending on your team availability.

[40:00] Maya: One more question — licensing for Dedicated vs Hosted?
[40:04] Diego: Hosted is usage-based; Dedicated is reserved capacity with monthly/annual commit that'll lower unit price. Private has a platform fee for the control plane. I can send pricing tiers.

[42:15] (Diego walks through example parity spreadsheet rows)
[42:30] Diego: Example mapping row: source_provider=OpenAI, source_model=gpt-4o-mini, redwood_model=redwood-4o-mini-q8, prompt_shim=prepend "[REDWOOD-compat]" and remove system token duplication, expected_delta_notes=slight punctuation differences in multi-turn json outputs.

[46:20] Raj: For function calls with nested args — you said schema helps; can you auto-validate?

[46:25] Liam: Console can run JSON schema validations as part of the eval harness. You can flag mismatches and auto-roll back via route policies.

[48:10] Maya: Anything else we should know about TogetherAI migrations?
[48:15] Diego: Together models emphasize open weights; mapping is model-specific. We often recommend running those models in a Dedicated or Private environment to control latency variance.

[50:00] Hannah: Okay, recap — next steps: we send parity sheet, you send prompts and sample traces, we provision a staging key and run an eval, then meet for POC kickoff.
[50:12] Maya: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[50:20] (Some informal sign-offs)
[51:00] Diego: I'll drop the links: parity spreadsheet, SOC2 + security whitepaper, benchmark script repo.
[51:10] Raj: Thanks.

[53:00] (Call ends)

Notes: transcription has expected ASR artifacts — proper nouns sometimes garbled (example: "redwood-4o" transcribed as "red wood four oh" in one spot). This file will be attached to the CRM and the parity spreadsheet will be the canonical artifact for the migration POC.
